audience.notes: Sophie and Marcus (Sydney, 30s, AUD 150K+, 70 to 110 guests), destination-minded: they may marry in Australia, abroad, or legally at home with the celebration overseas. ADAPTED FEARS for this legal topic (same approach as the Greece brief): fear A, from 'planning from the other side of the world', becomes 'we miss a legal deadline or sign the wrong thing while we are busy or travelling, and the marriage is not valid'; fear B, from 'budget and contracts', becomes 'we pay for a beautiful wedding that turns out not to be a legal marriage, or the paperwork breaks down between celebrant, registry and an overseas venue'. These are the top two fears for this piece. Paying parent (advisory): 'the marriage not being legally valid in Australia' answered with Attorney-General's Department wording. Anti-persona: PAA asks 'cheapest quickest way to get married'; answer official fees factually and briefly, never frame registry ceremonies or DIY as a way to save money.

payload.search_intent: Informational. Searchers expect a licence (US mental model, sometimes reinforced by snippets quoting 'county clerk'). They want to know if they need one, what to lodge, when, with whom, what it costs, and what changes if they marry overseas.
payload.angle: Answer first, then plan. Australia has no marriage licence: the legal step is the Notice of Intended Marriage, given to an authorised celebrant at least one month before the wedding (research batch A confirms exact wording, the maximum window, remote witnessing and shortening of time). The pillar covers every state in one place, then serves the destination-minded couple no ranking page serves: three legal routes (legal in Australia; legal at home plus a ceremony abroad; legal overseas with recognition at home) and a paperwork timeline counted back from the wedding date, showing the invisible coordination between celebrant, registry, venue and guests.
serp_gaps_to_win: Snippet answer in the first 60 words: 'Australia does not issue a marriage licence. The legal step is the Notice of Intended Marriage (NOIM)...' (Melbourne PAA asks this verbatim; #1 Sydney result wins with the same idea from a Perth celebrant page).
National, all-states explainer with a registry table (NSW, VIC, QLD, WA, SA, TAS, ACT, NT): SERPs show one state per page.

Clear, officially sourced timing: minimum notice, maximum window, shortening of time, remote witnessing, NOIM signed overseas. Snippets conflict (one month to 180 days vs 18 months); resolve with AGD.
Ceremonial vs official (registry-issued) marriage certificate and who lodges the paperwork after the ceremony; links to name change.

Destination routes: legal at home plus ceremony abroad, legal abroad with recognition in Australia; links to our Italy and Greece legal guides and the overseas certificate article. No ranking page connects the two.
Backward timeline for a 70 to 110 guest wedding (celebrant booking, NOIM, documents, interstate or overseas signing, final declaration, certificate order).

outline.h2: Do you need a marriage licence in Australia?
outline.answers: The search itself. No licence exists; the NOIM is the legal step. Snippet-ready.
must_include: First two sentences answer directly: no marriage licence in Australia; you give a Notice of Intended Marriage to your authorised celebrant (source: AGD 'Get married' and NOIM publication pages; batch A).
One line explaining why people search 'licence' (US, UK and NZ systems use licences or notices at a registrar); no detail on those systems.
The legal basis named plainly: Marriage Act 1961 and Marriage Regulations 2017 (AGD).
Key takeaways block (3 to 5 specific sentences) directly after the intro.

outline.h2: The Notice of Intended Marriage: when, how and who witnesses it
outline.answers: Everything about the NOIM: the one-month minimum, the maximum window, how it is signed and witnessed, and the rare exceptions.
must_include: Minimum notice and maximum validity window exactly as AGD states them (batch A). Do not repeat the '180 days' snippet unless AGD supports it.

Who may witness, in person and remotely, and the rule for a NOIM signed outside Australia (consular officer or notary; no remote witnessing for people outside Australia, per SERP snippets, to be verified by batch A).
Shortening of time: what it is, who grants it, that it is for exceptional circumstances; no promise it will be granted.
Where to get the official form (AGD); warn against outdated PDFs.
NOIM terms used naturally: 'notice of intended marriage', 'NOIM', 'NOIM form'.

outline.h2: Who can marry, and the documents you will need
outline.answers: Eligibility and the evidence a celebrant must see.
must_include: Eligibility in plain words (age, not already married, prohibited relationships, real consent) from AGD.
Evidence table: date and place of birth, identity, proof a prior marriage has ended (divorce order or death certificate), translations for foreign documents; source AGD (batch A).
Same-sex couples: marriage equality since 2017, one line from AGD.
Name spelling consistency across passport, birth certificate and NOIM, as practical advice.

outline.h2: State by state: registries, registry ceremonies and certificates
outline.answers: What differs between NSW, VIC, QLD and the other states and territories.
must_include: Table: state or territory | registry (BDM) | official certificate ordering | registry ceremony option | official link. Data from research batch B only.
Federal law is the same everywhere; registration and certificates are run by each state (batch A and B).
Registry ceremony fees only as official figures with date and source; no fee comparisons framed as savings.
Note that private businesses with names like 'marriage office' or 'marriage registry' are not government registries (factual, no names).

outline.h2: On the day and after: vows, signatures and your marriage certificate
outline.answers: What makes the ceremony legal, what you sign, and how to get the certificate you actually use.
must_include: Legal requirements of the ceremony (authorised celebrant, witnesses, required words) per AGD; batch A.
Declaration signed before the ceremony and the marriage register on the day (batch A to confirm names and timing).
Ceremonial certificate vs the official certificate from the state registry; who lodges the paperwork and the deadline (batch A/B); how to order the official one (batch B).
Name change: certificate as proof for passport and driver licence (bdm.vic.gov.au snippet; batch B for other states); one or two lines.

outline.h2: Marrying overseas, or legally at home with the celebration abroad
outline.answers: The destination-minded couple's three routes and how Australian law treats each.
must_include: Route 1: legal in Australia, then the celebration abroad (symbolic ceremony). Why many couples choose it; no judgement.

Route 2: legal overseas. Recognition of overseas marriages in Australia, sourced to AGD or Smartraveller (batch A), no legal advice beyond official wording. The Certificate of No Impediment from DFAT as what many countries ask for.
Route 3: a NOIM signed abroad for a wedding in Australia (overseas-based couple or one partner abroad), cross-reference to the witnessing rule in H2 2.
Links: our Italy legal guide, our Greece licence guide (only once published; else omit), and our overseas marriage certificate article. Descriptive anchors.
'Requirements vary by country and change; confirm with the destination's authorities and for your own passports.'

outline.h2: Your paperwork timeline, counted back from the wedding date
outline.answers: When to do each step for a 70 to 110 guest wedding. This is the invisible-work section and answers adapted fear A.
must_include: Backward timeline labelled as an example, not legal advice: book celebrant; sign NOIM (inside the official window, ideally well before the minimum); gather documents; overseas or interstate signing if needed; final declaration; ceremony; certificate order; name changes.

The coordination nobody sees: celebrant availability on the chosen date, venue and celebrant confirming the legal ceremony fits the run sheet, wet-weather plan that keeps witnesses and signing table in place, guests travelling interstate or from abroad.
For couples marrying overseas: when Australian documents (CNI, apostilles) need to be ordered relative to the trip; link to the country guides.
No guarantee language about dates or approvals.

outline.h2: What you handle, and where a Wedded Advisor helps
outline.answers: Who does what, so nothing legal falls between celebrant, registry and venue. Answers adapted fear B and the paying parent.
must_include: You must do personally: sign the NOIM and declaration, provide documents, choose a celebrant.

Where an advisor helps: matching the celebrant and venue to the legal and ceremony plan, timing the paperwork against travel and guest arrivals, destination legal routes, getting certificates home. Concierge framing from brand-profile only; no concierge prices.
Wedded World one line: link /wedded-world (Melbourne ended 8 Nov 2026); no ticket push.
Closing discovery_call CTA.
